title: Pattern: Handling Large Blobs
summary: Keep large files off your servers: presigned direct uploads, multipart resume, chunk dedup, pending-to-complete metadata states and CDN downloads.
body:
Any time a design stores photos, videos, documents or backups, someone has to move bytes that are thousands of times larger than a typical API request. If those bytes flow through your application servers, a single 2 GB upload ties up a request thread, a socket and memory for minutes, and your API fleet ends up sized for bandwidth instead of logic. This pattern shows up in file-sync, video, chat-attachment and social-media questions. The interviewer is checking that you keep large payloads off the request path, keep metadata and bytes consistent, and serve downloads from the edge.

## Separate the control plane from the data plane

The core move is to split the system in two. Your **application service** owns metadata: who owns the file, its name, size, content type, state and permissions. A **blob store** (an object store such as S3, GCS or Azure Blob Storage) owns the bytes. The client asks the application for permission, then talks to the blob store directly using a **presigned URL**: a URL that embeds a signature, an expiry and a constrained operation (for example "PUT this exact key, max 5 GB, valid for 15 minutes"). The blob store validates the signature itself, so your servers never touch the payload.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant API as File API
    participant DB as Metadata DB
    participant S3 as Blob store
    participant Q as Event queue
    C->>API: POST /files (name, size, sha256)
    API->>DB: insert file row, status=pending
    API-->>C: fileId + presigned PUT URL
    C->>S3: PUT bytes using presigned URL
    S3-->>C: 200 OK
    S3->>Q: object-created event
    Q->>API: consume event
    API->>DB: status=complete, record size and etag
```

The client first registers intent. The API writes a `pending` row and returns a short-lived presigned URL scoped to one object key it chose (never let the client pick arbitrary keys). The client uploads straight to the blob store. When the object lands, the store emits an object-created notification, and a consumer flips the row to `complete` after verifying size and checksum. The client may also call `POST /files/{id}/complete`, but treat that as a hint: clients crash, lose connectivity or lie, so the storage event (or a server-side `HEAD` on the object) is the source of truth.

### Multipart and resumable uploads

A single PUT of 5 GB over a mobile network will fail somewhere in the middle, and restarting from byte zero is miserable. Object stores support **multipart upload**: the client initiates an upload, sends parts independently (S3 parts are 5 MiB to 5 GiB, up to 10,000 parts), possibly in parallel, then calls complete with the list of part ETags. Failed parts are retried alone. The server presigns each part URL, and the upload ID plus the list of acknowledged parts is enough to resume after a crash. Incomplete multipart uploads still consume billable storage, so configure a lifecycle rule to abort them after a few days.

### Chunking and content-hash deduplication

File-sync products go further: they split files into fixed or content-defined chunks (commonly 4 MB), hash each chunk with SHA-256, and store chunks by hash. Before uploading, the client sends the list of chunk hashes and the server replies with the ones it does not have. Benefits: editing one byte of a 1 GB file re-uploads one chunk, identical files across users are stored once, and resume is free because each chunk is independently committed. Costs: a chunk index that can reach billions of rows, reference counting for garbage collection, and a privacy concern. Cross-user dedup lets an attacker test whether someone else has a given file by watching whether the upload is skipped, so many systems dedup only within a user or tenant.

## Keep metadata and bytes consistent

There is no transaction spanning your database and the blob store, so you must design for every partial outcome.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P["pending"] -->|"object event and checksum OK"| C["complete"]
    P -->|"no object after TTL"| E["expired"]
    P -->|"checksum mismatch"| F["failed"]
    C -->|"user deletes"| D["deleted"]
    E --> G["GC job removes row and any object"]
    F --> G
    D --> G
```

Files move through explicit states. Only `complete` files are listed or downloadable. A pending row whose object never arrives expires after a TTL (say 24 hours). A sweeper also handles the reverse case, an object with no matching row, by listing recent keys under the upload prefix and deleting orphans. Deletes are usually soft first (`deleted`, hidden from users) and reclaimed later, which gives you an undo window and lets the garbage collector run off-peak. If you dedup chunks, only collect a chunk when its reference count reaches zero and no in-flight upload references it.

## Serve downloads from the edge

Downloads mirror uploads. The API authorizes the request and returns a **signed URL** for a CDN (or the bucket directly for rarely accessed data). The CDN caches popular objects near users; the origin bucket can be private, readable only by the CDN. Keep signed URL lifetimes short (minutes) for private content; for public, immutable content, use content-addressed keys (`/v/sha256.mp4`) so caches never need invalidation.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U["Client"] -->|"1. GET /files/id"| API["File API (authz)"]
    API -->|"2. signed CDN URL"| U
    U -->|"3. GET with Range"| CDN["CDN edge"]
    CDN -->|"cache miss"| O[("Private bucket")]
```

The client gets a signed URL from the API, then fetches bytes from the nearest CDN edge, which falls back to the private bucket on a miss. **HTTP range requests** (`Range: bytes=1048576-2097151`, answered with `206 Partial Content`) let clients resume interrupted downloads, download segments in parallel and seek inside video without fetching the whole file.

## Options and trade-offs

| Approach | Good for | Cost or risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Proxy uploads through API servers | Tiny files, inline validation | API fleet sized for bandwidth; long-held connections; poor resume |
| Single presigned PUT | Files up to roughly 100 MB on good networks | Whole-file retry on failure; S3 caps single PUT at 5 GB |
| Presigned multipart upload | Large files, flaky networks, parallelism | Client complexity; must abort stale uploads |
| Chunked, content-addressed storage | Sync clients, versioning, dedup | Chunk index scale, refcount GC, cross-user privacy leaks |
| Signed URLs via CDN | Popular or global downloads | Revocation only by expiry or key rotation; cache key design |

## Failure modes and common mistakes

- **Trusting the client's "done" call.** Mark files complete from storage events or a server-side check, and verify size and checksum.
- **Long-lived or over-broad presigned URLs.** A URL valid for a week that allows any key is a public write endpoint. Scope key, method, size and content type; keep expiry short.
- **Forgetting orphans.** Without TTL expiry and sweeper jobs, abandoned uploads leak storage forever.
- **Storing blobs in the database.** Large BLOB columns bloat backups and replication and evict hot pages from the buffer cache. Store a key, not bytes.
- **Event notifications as exactly-once.** Storage events can be delayed or duplicated, so the completion handler must be idempotent (conditional update `WHERE status='pending'`).
- **Ignoring post-processing.** Virus scanning, thumbnailing or transcoding happen after upload; that is a long-running task with its own states.

## How to use it in an interview

Say the split explicitly: "Metadata goes to our service and database; bytes go directly to object storage via presigned URLs; downloads go through a CDN." Then walk the state machine and the cleanup jobs. Numbers worth having: chunk or part size (5 to 16 MB), number of parts for your largest file, URL expiry, and the bandwidth you avoided. For example, 10,000 concurrent 1 GB uploads would be about 10 TB in flight through your servers; with presigned URLs your API handles only 10,000 small JSON calls. Expect follow-ups on resume after a crash, how dedup interacts with deletes and privacy, how you revoke access to an already-shared link, and how you would scan uploads for malware before making them visible.

## Interview exercise

Design the upload path for a photo-backup app where phones upload up to 2,000 photos (3 to 8 MB each) at once over unreliable cellular networks. Specify the API calls, how the app resumes after being killed, how you avoid storing a photo twice when the same user re-uploads it, and what a user sees in the gallery while a photo is still uploading.

keyTakeaways: Split metadata (your service and database) from bytes (object storage); clients move bytes directly using short-lived, narrowly scoped presigned URLs.
Multipart or chunked uploads make large transfers resumable and parallel; abort stale multipart uploads with lifecycle rules.
Model files as pending, complete, failed or deleted, and mark them complete from storage events or server-side checks, not the client's word.
Sweepers must clean up both pending rows without objects and objects without rows.
Serve downloads through a CDN with signed URLs and support HTTP range requests for resume and seeking.
